title: What Happens When You Drink an Energy Drink?
sources: FDA, 'Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine Is Too Much?' ('Generally, energy drinks have 54 to 328 milligrams of caffeine per 16 fluid ounces' (about a sixfold range); 'For most adults, the FDA has cited 400 milligrams a day' as an amount not generally associated with negative effects; signs of too much: heart palpitations, insomnia or sleep disruptions, jitters, nausea; 'Too much caffeine in children and teens can cause increased heart rate'; 'Medical experts advise against energy drinks for children and teens because of the levels of sugar and caffeine'): https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much

Cleveland Clinic Health Essentials, 'How To Quit Caffeine' ('The effects of caffeine can be felt as soon as 15 minutes after it's consumed'; 'Once in your bloodstream, caffeine stimulates your central nervous system'; 'Six hours after caffeine is consumed, half of it is still in your body'): https://health.clevelandclinic.org/how-to-quit-caffeine

Cleveland Clinic Health Essentials, 'How To Get Caffeine Out of Your System' ('Caffeine has a half-life (the time it takes to decrease by half) of five hours'; too much: jittery and shaky, increased heart rate/palpitations, insomnia): https://health.clevelandclinic.org/how-to-get-caffeine-out-of-your-system

Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, The Nutrition Source, 'Caffeine' ('Caffeine is absorbed within about 45 minutes after consuming, and peaks in the blood anywhere from 15 minutes to 2 hours'; 'It can remain in the blood anywhere from 1.5 to 9.5 hours'; 'Caffeine can block the effects of the hormone adenosine, which is responsible for deep sleep'; high amounts 'speed up heart rate'; AAP: no caffeine under 12, adolescents 12+ no more than 100 mg daily): https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/caffeine/

Tease (next video): DAN Europe Alert Diver, 'DAN Begins Reporting on Incident Collection of Breath-Hold Diving' (carbon dioxide is the primary trigger for the urge to breathe; low oxygen is a surprisingly weak trigger): https://alertdiver.eu/en_US/articles/dan-begins-reporting-on-incident-collection-of-breath-hold-diving/ ; US Naval Safety Command, 'Lessons Learned 20-19: Shallow Water Blackout': https://navalsafetycommand.navy.mil/Portals/29/LL%2020-19%20Shallow%20Water%20Blackout.pdf

American Heart Association newsroom, 'Energy drinks, stimulant products linked to cardiac arrest, heart attack in young adults' (Scientific Sessions 2026, Abstract MDP0323, Nov. 2, 2026; FDA adverse-event reports 2017-2025: caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements appeared disproportionately more often in reports of serious cardiovascular events; 'research abstract... not peer-reviewed... preliminary'; an outside expert: 'the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events'): https://newsroom.heart.org/news/energy-drinks-stimulant-products-linked-to-cardiac-arrest-heart-attack-in-young-adults

lines.text: What happens when you drink an energy drink?
Five hours later: a quarter of the caffeine left, or half? Guess.
lines.caps: FIVE *HOURS LATER | A *QUARTER OF | THE *CAFFEINE LEFT, | OR *HALF? | *GUESS

lines.text: Some cans: fifty-four milligrams. Others: three twenty-eight.
Minute fifteen: you can already feel it.
Minute forty-five: it's blocking adenosine, your sleepy signal.
Ever had one on a late drive, then lay awake?
lines.caps: EVER HAD *ONE | ON A *LATE | *DRIVE, THEN | LAY *AWAKE?

lines.text: But here's the twist: it leaves slowly.
Too much? Jitters and a racing heart.
Most adults? The FDA cites four hundred a day.
Hour five: half is still in you. It's B.
Kids and teens? Experts say skip them.
